Adult female Flathead grey mullet (Mugil cephalus) in the Gulf of Mexico have been documented reaching an ultimate total length of ninety centimeters [Li = ninety centimeters], a substantial size that places them among the larger members of the family Mugilidae. Males attain a slightly smaller maximum length, with field surveys recording a comparable ultimate total length of eighty-eight centimeters [Li = eighty-eight centimeters], a dimorphism consistent with patterns observed in many coastal teleosts. This size disparity is reflected in the corresponding asymptotic body masses estimated from length-weight relationships. The ultimate wet weight for females approaches 7,660 grams [Wwi = 7,660 grams], while males reach approximately 7,160 grams [Wwi = approximately 7,160 grams], the latter representing a consistent but modest reduction in mass relative to the terminal size of females. These maximal dimensions are attained only after several years of sustained growth and represent the upper bound of the species’ morphological potential in temperate coastal habitats.

Puberty in this species is attained at a notably smaller size than the ultimate adult dimensions, marking the transition from a strictly somatic growth phase to one that includes reproductive allocation. Field studies indicate that the total length at puberty is 35.4 centimeters [Lp = 35.4 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a body mass of 479 grams [Wwp = 479 grams], derived from the regional length-weight conversion. This size at which gonadal maturation begins is a critical life-history parameter, reflecting the point at which individuals begin directing resources toward gamete production. At an environmental temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum reproductive rate has been estimated through empirical observation of spawning females. This rate, expressed in terms of annual egg output, amounts to approximately 1.1 million eggs per year [Ri = approximately 1.1 million eggs per year], a high fecundity typical of r-selected marine teleosts, and is realized through a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year] under those same thermal conditions.

The developmental biology of Mugil cephalus begins with the pelagic egg, which is small and buoyant, facilitating dispersal in coastal currents. Recent studies of ovarian histology have determined that the egg itself, prior to hydration and ovulation, has a diameter of about 0.9 millimeters, leading to an estimated wet weight per egg of 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a modest mass that nonetheless supports a fully developed yolk-sac larva upon successful fertilisation and subsequent eclosion. The incubation period is brief, and following hatching, the yolk-sac larva, or alevin stage, persists for a short duration before the onset of exogenous feeding. The timing of these early life-history events is tightly coupled to water temperature. Experimental rearing trials conducted under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] have further revealed that the maximum lifespan of this species is approximately 2,190 days [am = approximately 2,190 days], a longevity that reflects a relatively slow pace of life for a fast-growing, highly fecund coastal fish.

In relation to the reproductive ecology of this species, spawning events are typically triggered by environmental cues such as seasonal temperature shifts and lunar cycles, with peak activity often coinciding with periods when water temperatures approach 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the same thermal regime at which the maximum reproductive rate has been characterised. The high fecundity, coupled with the relatively small egg size, is a classic life-history strategy among r-selected marine fishes. From a comparative perspective, the pubertal length of 35.4 centimeters [Lp = 35.4 centimeters] found in Flathead grey mullet is not markedly different from that of congeneric species in the Indo-Pacific, though the ultimate sizes attained by females in the Mugil cephalus complex can vary substantially across distinct populations. Data from estuarine populations along the Atlantic coast of the United States indicate that the ultimate total length for females frequently reaches 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters], although individuals over 80 centimeters are not encountered annually, suggesting that such extreme longevity is only achieved under particularly favourable foraging conditions.

Physiological and ecological studies of Mugil cephalus further highlight the species’ role as a key link in coastal food webs, where its detritivorous and planktivorous feeding habits contribute to nutrient cycling. The combination of a high reproductive output of approximately 1.1 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1.1 million eggs per spawning event] and a rapid early growth rate allows this species to maintain robust populations despite variable recruitment success. Throughout their lifespan of approximately six years (2,190 days) [am = 2,190 days] under the thermal conditions typical of subtropical estuaries, these fish exhibit a remarkable capacity for somatic growth, with individuals exceeding 60 centimeters in total length commonly observed in productive nursery habitats at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The species’ broad environmental tolerance and high reproductive output underpin its successful global distribution across tropical and temperate marine coastlines.
